name: Trehalose

lead: Trehalose is a sugar that many organisms use to survive drying and stress. It is added to some moisturizers and serums as a water-binding, protective ingredient for hydrated, healthier-looking skin, and is discussed in anti-aging circles for its link to autophagy.

It stabilises proteins and membranes during dehydration. In mammalian cells it has been reported to trigger autophagy, partly through the TFEB pathway, though the mechanism is debated. Those findings come largely from cell and animal models of neurodegeneration, and small human trials are registered. No study found tests it for appearance.

paras: People encounter it in foods, dry-eye drops and cosmetic products where it is listed as a moisturizing ingredient. In skincare it is applied topically as part of a hydrating routine.
It is broken down to glucose by trehalase and is generally treated as safe in foods. Trehalase deficiency is uncommon, and a link to C. difficile outbreaks was disputed by a 2019 study.

angle.text: Trehalose binds water and protects cells from drying stress, so skin looks more hydrated and healthier. Its autophagy findings come from lab and animal research.

lead: Trehalose is a non-reducing disaccharide made of two glucose units joined by an alpha,alpha-1,1 glycosidic bond. It occurs in bacteria, yeast, fungi, insects, invertebrates and plants but cannot be synthesised by vertebrates.[1][2]

Commercially it is used in food as a mildly sweet stabiliser (about 45 percent as sweet as sucrose), in biopharmaceutical formulations, and in eye drops for dry eye.[1][2] Cosmetic uses as a moisturizing and protective ingredient are reported, but the encyclopedic sources reviewed do not cover them in detail.
Research interest in trehalose centres on its induction of autophagy in neurodegeneration models; small human trials are registered, but no study found tests it for appearance.[3][4]
infobox: Broken down by trehalase to glucose[1]

paras: The glycosidic bond makes trehalose highly resistant to acid hydrolysis and means its closed structure does not glycate proteins.[1] Anhydrous trehalose melts at 203 degrees Celsius.[1]

In many organisms it protects cells during drying and extreme conditions (anhydrobiosis), proposed to act by vitrification or by replacing water around membranes and proteins.[1][5] Insects use it as their main flight fuel and blood sugar.[1] In humans it is split into glucose by the intestinal enzyme trehalase; trehalase deficiency is uncommon but reported in about 10 to 15 percent of Greenlandic Inuit.[1]

H.A.L. Wiggers found trehalose in ergot of rye in 1832, and in 1859 Marcellin Berthelot isolated it from trehala manna and named it.[1] A 2007 paper reported it as an mTOR-independent autophagy enhancer,[3] and 2017 work showed it induces autophagy through TFEB.[1]

In food it is used in frozen products such as ice cream because it lowers freezing point.[1] It is an ingredient, with hyaluronic acid, in an artificial tears product for dry eye.[1] Grokipedia also reports use as a stabiliser in biopharmaceutical formulations, which is unverified AI-generated text.[2]

No studies found testing trehalose for appearance, skin or hair outcomes. Registered human studies address other conditions, including spinocerebellar ataxia type 3,[6] Parkinson disease,[7] Alzheimer disease,[8] bipolar depression,[9] non-alcoholic fatty liver,[10] acute coronary syndrome[11] and dry eye.[12] Several are small, unknown in status, withdrawn or have no published results in the sources reviewed.
Laboratory work includes the 2007 cell and mouse study of autophagy and clearance of mutant huntingtin and alpha-synuclein.[3]
Earlier reports linked dietary trehalose to Clostridioides difficile outbreaks, but a 2019 study disputed the association.[1]
